extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political science, public policy, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for how public opinion is produced, managed, and used by leaders — including how policies should be presented, how consent is manufactured, and what informational and analytic supports realistic opinion requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive policy addresses remote/uninteresting factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive policy deals with remote and uninteresting factors, rather than concentrating on visible, immediate incidents (e.g., smiting a greedy landlord) which attract popular interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders and legislatures often prefer visible targets even though systemic wastes or remote causes are more important; effective policy requires tackling causes that are less dramatic and less immediately visible. Example: instead of symbolic punishment of a landlord, increase housing supply to address shortages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect new policy to prevailing popular feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new policy is to be launched, all that the feeling of the mass demands is that the policy as it is developed and exposed shall be, if not logically, then by analogy and association, connected with the original feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial messaging should vocalize and identify with the audience's familiar attitudes (stories, patriotism, grievances) to create a 'community of feeling' before setting out the substantive plan; slogans alone will not contain the plan's substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trusted spokespeople and accepted symbols to secure consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Trusted men in a familiar role subscribing to the accepted symbols can go a very long way on their own initiative without explaining the substance of their programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar, credible figures and symbolic cues can obtain assent even when substantive explanation is lacking; this is strategically useful but can mask lack of justification for policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek measured consent by preparing subordinates and intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise leaders, provided publicity and debate will not be too damaging, seek a measure of consent by taking subordinates of the hierarchy into confidence to prepare them and make them feel they have freely willed the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation builds perceived voluntariness and reduces opposition, but such consultations may create illusions because most of the public cannot appreciate complex contingencies; leaders should balance openness with practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not arouse feelings you cannot channel into policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The statesman sees to it that he arouses no feeling which he cannot sluice into a program that deals with the facts to which the feelings refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demagogy provides temporary relief by expressing feeling but is dangerous if repeated; leaders should avoid stirring emotions that cannot be translated into constructive, factual programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders manage access to facts and act as censors/propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Every official is in some degree a censor... every leader is in some degree a propagandist; strategically a leader chooses what facts, in what setting, in what guise he shall permit the public to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials balance institutional safety and candor; information is framed and selected to shape public understanding. This is a strategic responsibility, not merely deception, and must weigh competing ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of consent is a technical, analytical art
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of consent has improved enormously in technic because it is now based on analysis rather than on rule of thumb; persuasion has become a self-conscious art and a regular organ of popular government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern persuasion draws on psychological research and mass communication; its refinements alter political calculations and premises and can be used without sinister intent but with powerful effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on intuition; use record, measurement, and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been demonstrated that we cannot rely upon intuition, conscience, or the accidents of casual opinion if we are to deal with the world beyond our reach; the inventions of measurement, record, quantitative and comparative analysis, and psychological analysis are key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realistic public opinion formation requires empirical methods and analytical tools; without them, decisions are vulnerable to self-deception and unverifiable persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic opinion requires resources and disciplined effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The working out of realistic opinion takes time, money, labor, conscious effort, patience, and equanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casual opinion, produced by partial contact and tradition, resists systematic improvement; developing reliable public opinion needs institutional investment and habits of self-criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expression and suggestion harden and polarize feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: A mass exposed to the same stimuli would develop responses that could be charted... when the vague feelings of those who felt vaguely had been put into words, they would know more definitely what they felt, and would then feel it more definitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated suggestion and verbalization shape group boundaries and intensify opinions; reporters and communicators who 'lead' can therefore create and harden public positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize organizers of opinion as skilled technicians
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been skilled organizers of opinion who understood the mystery well enough to create majorities on election day; these organizers possess effective knowledge about creating and operating public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss opinion organizers as mere 'problems'—they hold practical expertise in shaping public consent and should be studied rather than ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend the public's range of attention by reporting unseen environments
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of bringing any aspect of human affairs within the range of judgment (through continuous reporting) breaks the spell which has lain upon political ideas; continuous reporting of an unseen environment is feasible and can be improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing distant, complex events into public judgment (via journalism, reports, technical analysis) enables more informed democratic choice; quality and honesty of reporting matter for democratic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible attempts to address grievances reduce risk of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If the established powers are sensitive and well-informed, if they are visibly trying to meet popular feeling, and actually removing some of the causes of dissatisfaction, no matter how slowly they proceed, they have little to fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception of progress and responsiveness diminishes revolutionary pressure from below; palace or demagogic revolutions remain different risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political survival often involves small favors and symbolic acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The mending of fences consists in offering an occasional scapegoat, redressing a minor grievance affecting a powerful individual or faction, rearranging certain jobs, placating a group who want local projects, or a law to stop somebody's vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many elected officials prefer doing small, tangible services for many people rather than attempting large, abstract reform; attention to influential or dramatically powerless constituencies is a tactical choice.
